levels of love: wife, daughter, mother

title.en: Introductions and thanks

summary.en: Other speakers thank the yeshiva's supporters and introduce the Mashgiach, mostly in English. The Mashgiach then greets the audience and asks permission to speak sitting.

title.en: Elul and the seventh consolation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'Ani l'dodi v'dodi li' grows stronger as Rosh Hashanah nears, and that in the seventh haftarah of consolation Klal Yisrael finally answers Hashem as a bride. He recalls the piyut 'Anu ra'yasecha v'atah dodenu' and adds its next line, 'Anu vanecha v'atah avinu', then brings 'Vatomer Tziyon' and 'Hatishkach isha ulah'.

title.en: The broken luchos and forgetting

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Berachos that the golden calf will be forgotten but Sinai will not, and the teaching that the breaking of the luchos brought forgetting. With the Maharal and the Midrash on the luchos' six handbreadths he shows that the luchos were the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and asks why, if forgetting prevailed for the calf, it did not prevail for Sinai.

title.en: Daughter, sister, mother: a bond that holds

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers from the start of the passuk and the Midrash on 'ba'atarah she'itrah lo imo': a king calls his beloved daughter 'my sister', 'my daughter' and finally 'my mother'. A wife's bond can be severed, a daughter's cannot but can know anger, and a mother's love for her infant knows none. With the parable of a hospital's backup generator he explains that when the calf cut the bond of bride and groom, the higher levels remained.

title.en: Klal Yisrael is terumah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a Gemara about an esrog of terumah, where the Amora declares sharply that terumah has no redemption, and asks why he speaks with such zeal. He answers with the Midrash of the king who sends away his queen and orders her a necklace, with 'Kodesh Yisrael laShem reishis tevuasoh' and with Rashi in Nitzavim: Jews are terumah and cannot be exchanged, and the claim that they were exchanged is Bilaam's.

title.en: Rotzeh ani, Yom Kippur and Simchas Torah

summary.en: Bringing the Rambam, the Mashgiach explains that a Jew's heart is never with the sin, and that Yom Kippur, equal in gematria to 'rotzeh ani', expresses each Jew's will. He traces the rising levels from the last haftarah through Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur to Shemini Atzeres, whose guest is Shlomo HaMelech, and explains why Simchas Torah ends with the breaking of the luchos and at once begins Bereishis.

title.en: The yeshiva's purpose and blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach sums up the rising levels of the coming days and says the gathering is to show that Jews do not forget Matan Torah, through yeshivos, Torah and mitzvos. He thanks those who came and supported the yeshiva and blesses them with a good year; another speaker then announces a presentation.

catalogTitle: נשים: מיר דארפן זיך האלטן שטארק אין די אמעריקאנע בית לבן

oneLiner.en: From Eliezer, who needed Avraham's oath to stay upright in Lavan's house, the Mashgiach teaches that today the whole world, and America above all, is Lavan's house, and that Jewish families must hold strong in tznius and keep growing.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why Avraham had to make Eliezer, his great and devoted disciple, swear an oath. He explains the power of an oath: shevuah is related to sheva, seven, and binds a person's seven middos to Hashem's Name, and mashbia shares a root with mashpia, an infusion of strength from Heaven. A story of the Vizhnitzer Rebbe shows that every soul swears before birth to be a tzaddik. Lavan's house was the headquarters of the Satan, and Eliezer, who had a personal interest, needed the oath to stay upright there. Today, the Mashgiach says, the world and especially America is Lavan's house, and he lists ways to hold strong. He brings the Divrei Yechezkel on the clothes Eliezer gave Rivka and the clothes Hashem made for Adam and Chava. He closes with Chanukah's lesson of constant growth, a teshuvah of the Chasam Sofer, and hachnasas kallah.

en: Avraham made even Eliezer, a great talmid chacham and devoted disciple, swear before sending him to find a match for Yitzchak.
An oath binds a person's seven middos to Hashem's Name and draws strength from Heaven to do His will.
Lavan's house was the headquarters of the Satan, and to stay upright there even Eliezer needed the kedushah of the oath.
Today the whole world, and especially America, is Lavan's house, and it is very hard to keep tznius and kedushah in it.
Like the Chanukah lights that keep increasing, a Jew and a Jewish couple must always keep growing better.

title.en: Why Eliezer had to swear

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the parsha: Avraham sends Eliezer to find a wife for Yitzchak and first makes him swear. He describes Eliezer as a great talmid chacham who taught Avraham's Torah and risked his life for his rebbe, and asks why such a person needed an oath.

title.en: The power of an oath

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that a soul is made to swear before birth to be a tzaddik, and explains that shevuah comes from sheva, the seven middos, and that mashbia is related to mashpia. He tells how the Vizhnitzer Rebbe wept on Rosh Hashanah night at the words 'lo nishba l'mirmah' and explained it as the soul's oath.

title.en: Lavan's house, headquarters of the Satan

summary.en: Citing the Zera Kodesh, the Mashgiach describes the house of Besuel and Lavan as the headquarters of the sitra achra, where the tumah was so strong that one had to thank Hashem for not sinning. Since Eliezer had a personal interest, wanting his own daughter for Yitzchak, he needed the holy influence of Avraham's oath to stay upright there.

title.en: America today is Lavan's house

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that before Moshiach a great tumah comes into the world, and today the whole world, especially America, is Lavan's house. He contrasts this with America of seventy years ago, showing the old public school buildings in Williamsburg with separate doors for boys and girls, and praises families who still live with tznius and kedushah, the Eliezers of today.

title.en: How to hold strong in Lavan's house

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists what keeps a Jew strong: attachment to tzaddikim, a rav for every family's questions, gatherings for chizuk, mussar seforim and erliche friends. He speaks of the endless new 'keilim' of the yetzer hara, and of last week's storm, bringing Rashi that immorality brings destruction that strikes good and bad alike, and the Gemara that tzaddikim suffer first. He ends with the struggle of Jewish daughters against today's styles.

title.en: Clothes for Rivka and for Adam and Chava

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Divrei Yechezkel's question how Eliezer knew Rivka's size when he brought her clothes, and his answer that he brought a sample of the clothing worn in Avraham's house. He then asks why Hashem made garments for Adam and Chava when they had already made coverings, and explains that Hashem showed what clothing He is pleased with.

title.en: Chanukah's growth and hachnasas kallah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah's 'mosif v'holech' teaches constant growth, and brings a teshuvah of the Chasam Sofer that a wife cannot object that her husband became more stringent. He praises the tznius of the women's section of the beis medrash, says a woman dressed less modestly should not be rebuked but helped with grace, and closes with hachnasas kallah and a brachah.

catalogTitle: אמונה - יסוד של כל המצוות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why emunah, the first mitzvah of the heart, is not just one mitzvah among the 613 but the foundation on which all of them stand.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the order of the Sefer Chareidim, which arranges the mitzvos by the limbs of the body and begins with the heart; its first mitzvah is emunah, from the verse 'Anochi Hashem Elokecha'. The 613 mitzvos build the body with which a person will rise at techiyas hameisim, so one who lacks emunah, a mitzvah of the heart, cannot rise at all. Yaakov's request for bread and a garment hints at Torah as the soul's food and mitzvos as its garments in the next world. He discusses gilgul and how learning about a mitzvah one cannot keep counts for it. He brings the Gemara in Makkos that Chavakuk based all the mitzvos on emunah, then the dispute whether emunah is counted among the 613: the Ramban compares it to a building's basement. Every mitzvah is a command, but 'Anochi' is a statement, and it names the exodus from Egypt, which the whole people saw.

en: The Sefer Chareidim orders the mitzvos by the limbs, beginning with the heart, and the first mitzvah of the heart is emunah.
Each limb is built for techiyas hameisim by the mitzvah connected to it, and without emunah, a mitzvah of the heart, a person cannot rise at all.
Torah is the soul's food in Gan Eden and the mitzvos are its garments.
The Rishonim dispute whether emunah is counted among the 613; the Ramban holds it is not, because it is their foundation, like the basement of a building.
Every mitzvah, even those of the heart, is given as a command, but 'Anochi Hashem Elokecha' is worded as a statement.
Jewish emunah is based on the exodus from Egypt, where the whole people saw that Hashem controls nature.

title.en: Sefer Chareidim: the heart and the first mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Sefer Chareidim orders the mitzvos by the limbs, starting with the heart, whose first mitzvah is emunah. He explains that the 613 mitzvos build the body for techiyas hameisim, so a person without emunah cannot rise, and mentions the garment made of the mitzvos.

title.en: Bread and garment: Torah and mitzvos

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yaakov, in danger, asked only for bread and a garment, and answers that in the next world Torah is the soul's food and mitzvos its garments. He discusses gilgul for a mitzvah not yet kept, the mitzvos that cannot be kept in galus, and how learning about a mitzvah counts for it.

title.en: Why learn emunah; Chavakuk's one mitzvah

summary.en: Returning to emunah, the Mashgiach says that without it a Jew has no connection to the World to Come, and explains why the shiurim came to focus on this one mitzvah. He brings the Gemara in Makkos that Chavakuk based all the mitzvos on 'tzaddik be'emunaso yichyeh', and explains it means concentrating on one mitzvah through which all are kept.

title.en: Is emunah one of the 613? The basement

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Gemara does not list the 613, so the Rishonim counted them and disagree on some, emunah among them. The Rambam counts it; the Ramban does not, because it is the foundation of the mitzvos, like a basement that is not counted as a room yet holds the whole building. He adds that every mitzvah in the Torah is worded as a command.

title.en: A command to love; 'Anochi' and the exodus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that even love and fear of Hashem are commanded, since every Jew already loves Hashem and must only reveal it, whereas 'Anochi' is a statement, not a command. He asks why it mentions the exodus rather than creation, and answers that our emunah rests on the exodus, which the whole people saw.

catalogTitle: The מדה of הוד and its Connection to רשב”י

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why Lag BaOmer, hod shebehod and the day of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, belongs to every Jew: Rashbi, the Kohen Gadol of the hidden Torah, revealed that every Jew carries a hidden point in which he is irreplaceable.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach sets out to explain the Bnei Yissaschar's words that, just as Hashem is for everyone, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and Lag BaOmer are for everyone, even the lowest. Hod, the fifth middah, means yielding and is the Beis HaMikdash; Lag BaOmer, hod shebehod, is the Kodesh HaKodashim, a place above time, space and nature, and Rashbi, who revealed the hidden Torah, is the Kohen Gadol after the churban, whom mourning does not touch. The students of Rabbi Akiva did not honor one another because they did not see that every Jew, like every letter in the Sefer Torah, has a hidden point in which he is irreplaceable. The Mashgiach connects this to combining sedras in seasons of achdus, to stories of the Satmar Rav and the Arizal in Meron, to Purim, which is also hod, and to the 33rd letter of Baruch Shem and Shema.

en: Hod is the middah of yielding and is the Beis HaMikdash; its place is the Beis HaMikdash, its soul is Aharon and the kohanim, and its time is the week of Lag BaOmer.
Lag BaOmer, hod shebehod, is the Kodesh HaKodashim, above time, space and nature, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is the Kohen Gadol who enters it after the churban.
Every Jew corresponds to one of the 600,000 letters of the Sefer Torah and has a point in which he is irreplaceable and surpasses even the greatest tzaddik.
The students of Rabbi Akiva failed to honor one another because they did not see the hidden superiority of each friend; Rashbi revealed that every Jew has such a side.
In seasons tied to redemption a breach of achdus is graver, and so sedras are combined then, against the usual rule not to mix them.
Purim, like Lag BaOmer, is hod: both fall on the same day of the week, both are a mystery, and on both even the lowest Jew rejoices.

title.en: Hod: the Beis HaMikdash and Aharon

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Bnei Yissaschar that Lag BaOmer, like Hashem, is for everyone, even the lowest, and sets out to explain it. He brings the Gemara in Berachos that hod is the Beis HaMikdash, ties Lag BaOmer in parshas Emor to the kohanim and to Aharon, the fifth of the seven shepherds, and defines hod as yielding, like grass that bends in a storm.

title.en: The Kohen Gadol and the Kodesh HaKodashim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Sefirah mourning for Rabbi Akiva's students ends on Lag BaOmer because hod is the Beis HaMikdash, which mourning does not reach, as the Torah says the Kohen Gadol does not leave the Mikdash. Lag BaOmer, hod shebehod, is the Kodesh HaKodashim; he brings the Mishnah of the ten miracles and the Gemara that the place of the Aron took no space, and explains that time, space and arithmetic are earthly limits that do not apply there.

title.en: Rashbi, the Kohen Gadol after the churban

summary.en: Mentioning the Gemara in Yoma, the Mashgiach concludes that the Kodesh HaKodashim is above time, place and nature, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the joy of Lag BaOmer is above nature. After the churban there is still a Kohen Gadol who enters the Kodesh HaKodashim: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who revealed the hidden Torah, as the song Bar Yochai says.

title.en: Every Jew is a letter in the Sefer Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Rabbi Akiva's students, one of whom may truly have known more than his chavrusa, should have shown honor. He answers that, as there are 600,000 letters in the Torah and 600,000 souls, every Jew has a point no one else can replace, in which he surpasses even a great tzaddik; so a talmid chacham must honor even a simple Jew.

title.en: Words, families and kehillos: not mixing sedras

summary.en: The Mashgiach extends the parable: letters form words, which are families, and lines, columns and sedras are neighborhoods and kehillos. He brings the Magen Avraham that a sedra may not be read on a Shabbos that is not its own, compares this to each kehillah keeping its minhagim, and notes that at certain times sedras are combined.

title.en: What includes all: Shabbos, Rashbi, the Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the twelve tribes and months with the seven shepherds who include all of Klal Yisrael, the sea split into twelve at Krias Yam Suf and into seven in the future, and Rosh Chodesh fused with Shabbos. Rashbi, the Shabbos of the year, and the Beis HaMikdash include everything; the Beis HaMikdash was lost through sinas chinam, and the root of the divisions in Klal Yisrael is Yehudah and Yosef.

title.en: Combining sedras in seasons of achdus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in times when redemption is expected a breach of achdus is graver, so in four seasons (before Rosh Chodesh Nissan, the three weeks, Sefirah and before Rosh Hashanah) sedras are combined. He hints that the split of Yosef and Yehudah corresponds to Misnagdim and Chassidim, and illustrates it with the question whether a rav gets shishi or shlishi.

title.en: The sea's claim: shlishi against shishi

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the sea refused to split for Moshe, since it was created on the third day and man on the sixth, and Hashem rebuked it: at the redemption shishi and shlishi combine. The students of Rabbi Akiva did not see that each friend is superior in some hidden way; Rashbi, the Kohen Gadol of hod shebehod, revealed that every Jew has such a side, and so honor is due.

title.en: Melachah, curse and the sensitivity of Sefirah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Adam in Gan Eden did no melachah and that the 39 melachos come from the 39 curses, so on Shabbos, a day of blessing, melachah strikes at its essence. Likewise sinas chinam is worse in Sefirah, the walk toward the yovel of Shavuos and achdus; on Lag BaOmer Rashbi revealed the secret of each letter and soul, so the mourning stopped, as a Kohen Gadol has no mourning.

title.en: No mourning in Meron

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that the Satmar Rav, in Meron during the nine days, sang Bar Yochai since there is no mourning there, and brings from the writings of the Arizal the story of Rav Avraham HaLevi, punished for saying Nachem in Meron. From Meron the joy spreads, and he completes the Bnei Yissaschar's words: Rashbi reveals that even the lowest Jew carries a hidden point precious to Hashem.

title.en: Purim, Lag BaOmer and the point of the yud

summary.en: The Mashgiach maps the festivals onto the middos and shows that Purim is also hod, so even the lowest Jew rejoices on it, and that Lag BaOmer always falls on Purim's day of the week. Both are a mystery; counting the letters of Baruch Shem and then Shema, the 33rd letter is the first yud of Hashem's name, the point that contains everything, and he closes that what he grasps of Lag BaOmer is only that it is a secret.

catalogTitle: אמונה - ירושה מאבותינו הקדושים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jew's emunah is an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, an inborn trait like an animal's instinct, so the mitzvah is not to acquire it but not to spoil it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the dispute between the Rambam and the Ramban whether emunah is counted among the 613 mitzvos, and asks why the mitzvah of 'Anochi Hashem' is written as a statement and not as a command. To explain, he distinguishes acquired traits, such as knowledge and good habits, from hereditary ones, such as height and eye color, and shows from the instincts of spiders, beavers, birds and bees that even knowledge can be inherited. Emunah is such an inheritance: Jews are believers, sons of believers. A Jew who seems not to believe has a sick emunah, made ill mainly by forbidden foods and arayos, and must go to a tzaddik for a cure. Following Rav Tzadok HaKohen, the mitzvah is not to spoil this fact. He urges learning Chumash with Rashi and Ramban, and closes with the spark of Avraham in every Jew, guarded by Hashem as 'Magen Avraham'.

en: Some traits are acquired from outside, like knowledge and trained habits, while others pass by inheritance, like hair and eye color.
Animal instincts, like the spider's web and the bird's migration, show that even knowledge can be inherited.
A Jew's emunah in Hashem is an inheritance; Jews are 'believers, sons of believers'.
A Jew whose emunah is weak has made it sick, mainly through forbidden foods and arayos, and needs a tzaddik to heal him.
The mitzvah of emunah is written as a fact because Jews are born with it; the command is not to spoil it.
Every Jew carries a piece of Avraham Avinu within him, a spark that can never be extinguished.

title.en: Is emunah a mitzvah? Acquired and inherited traits

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the Rambam-Ramban dispute whether emunah is counted among the 613 mitzvos, and asks why 'Anochi Hashem' is written as a statement rather than a command. He begins his answer by distinguishing traits acquired from outside, like knowledge and trained habits, from hereditary ones, like height, eye color and hair color.

title.en: Inherited knowledge: instinct and emunah

summary.en: Knowledge itself normally comes from outside, but the Mashgiach shows from the spider's web, the beaver's dam, birds' migration and the bees' honeycomb that some knowledge is inherited. So it is no wonder that a Jew's emunah comes by inheritance, and Jews who do not believe have made their emunah sick.

title.en: Believers, sons of believers; healing a sick emunah

summary.en: From Moshe Rabbeinu's words 'they will not believe me' and Hashem's reply that they are believers, sons of believers, the Mashgiach shows that emunah, love and fear of Hashem are inherited from Avraham and Yitzchak. Where they are weak, the soul is sick, and as the Rambam says, it must be healed like the body: a man who ruined his appetite still has it and needs a doctor to restore it.

title.en: What sickens emunah, and the mitzvah not to spoil it

summary.en: Every sin weakens emunah, but especially questionable food and arayos, which clog the soul like cholesterol clogs the heart; the cure is to go to the tzaddik for a prescription of learning, davening and tzedakah. The Mashgiach then answers his opening question, developing Rav Tzadok HaKohen: the mitzvah is written as a fact because a Jew is born believing, and the command is not to spoil that fact.

title.en: The parshiyos of the Avos as the foundation of emunah

summary.en: Turning to the parshiyos about to be learned, beginning with Avraham's birth at the end of Noach, the Mashgiach says the stories of the Avos and Yetzias Mitzrayim are the foundation of emunah, and brings the Chasam Sofer that a Jew must regularly learn Chumash with Rashi and Ramban. Once emunah was absorbed at home and in the shtetl; today, when many shuls are social institutions, it must be drawn from the seforim.

title.en: The spark of Avraham in every Jew

summary.en: Emunah is inherited from Avraham Avinu, the first to truly believe, and the first mention of emunah in the Torah is his. With the parable of a tree containing all the trees that grow from its seeds, the Mashgiach explains that every Jew was once part of Avraham and carries a piece of him, a spark or pilot light that no waters can extinguish. He brings the Chiddushei HaRim that in 'Magen Avraham' we thank Hashem for guarding this point.

catalogTitle: טעם של כפירה הוא rationalization

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that kefirah is not a conclusion of the mind but a rationalization of the heart: a person who does not want to carry the Torah's demands fools himself with denial and invented reasons.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the teaching of tzaddikim that fooling oneself is worse than fooling others, since the one who deceives others at least knows the truth. Chazal read 'do not stray after your hearts' as minus, heresy: kefirah comes from the heart, the seat of desires, not from the mind. Psychology, a new science, names two forms of this self-deception. Denial: Chiel of Beis El kept building Yericho while his sons died one by one under Yehoshua's curse; the ostrich hides its head in the sand; the smoker insists cigarettes will not harm him. Rationalization: the ba'al gaavah invents reasons to defend his pride, the bochur blames everything but himself, the wolf calls the grapes sour. This, the Mashgiach says, is the secret of the apikores: Hashem is visible everywhere, but the Torah is too hard for them, so they build ever-changing theories of creation. Every Jew truly believes; old people return to teshuvah once their desires fade, while those driven by gaavah often do not.

en: Following the tzaddikim, the Mashgiach says one must guard even more against fooling oneself than against fooling others, because self-deception hides the truth even from the deceiver.
Chazal read 'after your hearts' as heresy: kefirah comes from the heart, the source of desires, and a person can fool himself because he has desires.
Denial means refusing to admit what a person knows deep down, as with Chiel of Beis El, the ostrich and the smoker.
Rationalization means inventing reasons to protect one's pride or desire, like the wolf who declared the grapes he could not reach to be sour.
The apikores denies creation not because the Torah's account makes no sense, but because the Torah's demands are too hard for him, so he builds his own theories.
Every Jew believes in the Ribono shel Olam even when he calls himself an apikores; he only denies it, and even a non-Jew can see Hashem through His deeds.

title.en: Fooling oneself and the heart's desires

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the Torah's ban on lying to others with the tzaddikim's warning against fooling oneself, and brings Chazal that 'after your hearts' means heresy, which grows from desires. He notes that psychology, a new science, sheds light on this, adding the Chazon Ish's reply that Chumash and Rashi already teach it.

title.en: Denial: Chiel, the ostrich and the smoker

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Chiel of Beis El rebuilt Yericho despite Yehoshua's curse, losing his sons one by one, and asks why he did not stop. The answer is denial, which he illustrates with the bird that buries its head in the sand and the smoker who insists his cigarette will not harm him.

title.en: Rationalization and the sour grapes

summary.en: The Mashgiach defines rationalization as inventing reasons to defend one's pride or desire: the ba'al gaavah who keeps his pride, the bochur who blames his chavrusa, rebbi and the room for not learning, the man who blames the hammer. He tells the fable of the wolf who could not climb the fence and declared the grapes sour.

title.en: Why apikorsim invent theories of creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why apikorsim, who inherited emunah and can see Hashem in nature, history and events, invent ever-changing theories of creation instead of accepting the Chumash. He recalls the evolution taught in his school days, and a frum chief physicist who refuted evolution from science to the yeshiva bochurim, and concludes that they deny because the Torah is too hard for them: the sour grapes again.

title.en: No true atheist: teshuvah, taivah and gaavah

summary.en: The Mashgiach argues that no apikores is truly certain; at most he has a doubt, which no one would gamble on, as with poisoned bottles. Old people do teshuvah once their desires fade, while those driven by gaavah often do not. He concludes that every Jew believes and even a non-Jew can see Hashem through His deeds, citing Reb Elchonon Wasserman that a kofer is liable because kefirah is rationalization.

catalogTitle: Why ל”ג בעומר is the עיקר day of ספירה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Sefirah and the month of Iyar are a time for achdus, for joining opposites into the harmony of Tiferes, and that Lag BaOmer, Hod sheb'Hod, is Tiferes sheb'Tiferes when counted from Hashem's side, the day of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai who binds all Jews together.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by asking why Parshas Kedoshim was said to all of Klal Yisrael together. He describes the 600,000 souls as the letters of the Sefer Torah, rising from letters to words, families and shevatim up to the Avos and Yerushalayim, where every Jew is joined to every other. The third week of Sefirah is Tiferes, the harmony that blends opposites such as chesed and gevurah, and the Tomer Devorah calls Torah Tiferes and every machlokes a blemish in it. Counted from Hashem's side, Lag BaOmer is Tiferes sheb'Tiferes. He then explains why sedras are combined at four times of the year: to repair sinas chinam, rooted in the strife of Yehuda and Yosef and in the diminishing of the moon. In a leap year the moon catches up with the sun, so no combining is needed. He ends with Iyar and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who unite all Jews, and with v'ahavta l'rei'acha kamocha.

en: The 600,000 Jewish souls are the letters of the Sefer Torah; they join into words, families and shevatim, up to the Avos, who contain all of Klal Yisrael.
On the Regalim a Jew is raised above his shevet to the level of the Avos, and in Yerushalayim, which belongs to no single shevet, all Jews are united.
Tiferes is harmony: two opposites, like chesed and gevurah, blended into a new and beautiful whole, and it is the main middah of Sefirah because Torah is Tiferes.
Counting from Malchus sheb'Malchus, Hashem's direction, Lag BaOmer is Tiferes sheb'Tiferes.
Sedras are combined at four times of the year to repair sinas chinam, which destroyed the Beis HaMikdash, the place of achdus.
The strife between Yehuda and Yosef goes back to the diminishing of the moon, and in a leap year, when the moon catches up with the sun, the sedras need not be combined.
Iyar and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai bind all Jews together, and Parshas Kedoshim, with v'ahavta l'rei'acha kamocha, was said when all of Klal Yisrael was gathered.

title.en: Kedoshim b'hakhel and the letters of the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what is special about Parshas Kedoshim, which Rashi says was said to all the Jews together, and speaks of Shabbos Mevarchim and Iyar, the month of Sefirah. He describes the 600,000 souls as the letters of the Sefer Torah, from Moshe Rabbeinu down to the forgotten Jew.

title.en: From letters to shevatim, Avos and Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach traces how individual letters join into words, families and shevatim, up to the Avos, and shows the same order in Eretz Yisrael, where Yerushalayim belongs to no single shevet. On the Regalim a Jew rises to the Avos, and the Yerushalmi treats every Jew in Yerushalayim as a chaver.

title.en: Tiferes as harmony of opposites

summary.en: Entering the week of Tiferes, the Mashgiach defines Tiferes as harmony: Yaakov merges the opposites of Avraham's chesed and Yitzchak's gevurah, like colors in a painting, husband and wife, or notes in a niggun. Citing the Tomer Devorah that Torah is Tiferes, he says Tiferes is the main middah of Sefirah.

title.en: Lag BaOmer as Tiferes sheb'Tiferes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Lag BaOmer is the noted day of Sefirah: Shavuos is the marriage of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and as the chassan goes out toward the kallah, Hashem counts from Malchus upward, so Hod sheb'Hod is Tiferes sheb'Tiferes. He brings the Tomer Devorah that every machlokes blemishes Tiferes except a machlokes l'shem shamayim, which ends in greater shalom.

title.en: Why sedras are combined four times a year

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Magen Avraham, from the Zohar, that sedras may not be mixed because each Shabbos and its sedra belong to a particular group of Jews, and asks why we nevertheless combine sedras at four times of the year. He answers that the Beis HaMikdash, the place of achdus, was destroyed by sinas chinam, so before Nisan, before Tishrei, in Sefirah and in the Three Weeks the barriers between Jews are broken.

title.en: Yehuda and Yosef: shlishi against shishi

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the two lines of leadership in Jewish history, Yehuda and Yosef, whose strife goes back to the kitrug of the moon, and their echo today between Sefardim and Ashkenazim and in which aliyah is most honored, shlishi or shishi. He brings the Midrash that the Yam Suf claimed seniority over Moshe, and explains that when Jews are in trouble there is no room for such quibbles.

title.en: The moon catches up in a leap year

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the haftarah's promise that the plowman will meet the reaper, which the Midrash reads as Yosef meeting Yehuda. He asks why in a leap year no sedras are combined during Sefirah and answers that the extra month lets the moon catch up with the sun, healing the diminishing of the moon, which is why the month is called Adar Sheni.

title.en: Iyar and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai unite all Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai binds all Jews together, so that at Meron, as at the Kosel, one sees every kind of Jew, and that Iyar is the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael. He returns to his opening question: Kedoshim, with v'ahavta l'rei'acha kamocha, unites all Jews and so was said to all of them together, and he ties Pesach Sheni and the mourning for Rabbi Akiva's students to the same theme.

catalogTitle: מאברהם אבינו התחיל אומה שמאמין בה'

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham and Sarah had to be barren so that with Avraham a new kind of being would begin, one that believes in Hashem by instinct, and that this emunah passes to every Jew as an inheritance through the mother.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach recalls that every Jew inherits his emunah from the Avos, so a denier is not a true heretic but is deceiving himself. He then asks why Avraham and Sarah had to be barren, since nothing in the world is chance; even the word 'mikreh' belongs to the language of impurity. Following the seforim, he explains that barrenness cut Avraham off from the chain of generations: a new creation began with him, a species that believes in Hashem as knowledge in the blood, not only in the mind. This is why Avraham was exempted from honoring his father, and why the world's creation was completed only with Avraham. A kofer, like the pitch on Noach's ark, merely covers over a belief that fills his whole body. Through the three matzos and four cups he shows that intellect comes from the father and feeling from the mother, so emunah, which is feeling, comes from the mother, as the word itself shows, and Jewishness follows the mother. Denial is rationalization, like Eisav blaming his wife.

en: Every Jew inherits emunah from the Avos; one who denies Hashem believes deep inside and is only trying to excuse himself.
Nothing in the world is chance, down to a cup of coffee or a straw moved by the wind; all is hashgacha pratis.
Avraham and Sarah had to be barren to cut them off from the previous generations, so that a new kind of being, one that believes in Hashem by instinct, could begin with them.
Emunah is not a matter of intellect but is part of the Jew's whole body, so a kofer only covers it over.
Intellect comes from the father and feeling from the mother; emunah, being feeling, comes from the mother, which is why a child's Jewishness follows the mother.
Denying Hashem is rationalization, as Eisav blamed his wife for losing the brachos instead of himself.

title.en: Inherited emunah and the barren Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that every Jew inherits emunah from the Avos and a denier only fools himself. He asks why Avraham and Sarah had to be barren, stressing that nothing is chance and that the word 'mikreh' is a language of impurity.

title.en: A new species begins with Avraham

summary.en: Bringing the Yismach Moshe, the Mashgiach explains that barrenness cut Avraham and Sarah off from the continuity of the generations, so that a new creation began with Avraham: a species that believes in Hashem by instinct.

title.en: Freed from honoring Terach; creation ends with Avraham

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Torah records Terach's death before Avraham leaves Charan, through the Midrash that Avraham was exempted from honoring his father, since he was a new species. From the pesukim said in the morning davening he shows that creation was completed with Avraham, whose heart was found faithful.

title.en: The kofer only covers over his belief

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the word 'kofer' from the pitch that covered Noach's ark and from the kofer hakol of the Gemara, who knows he owes the money: a denier only paints over his belief. Emunah, he says, is not in the brain but in the whole body.

title.en: Matzos and cups: emunah comes from the mother

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Seder has three matzos and four cups, and explains that grain gives intellect and corresponds to the Avos, while wine gives feeling and corresponds to the Imahos. Since emunah is feeling, it comes from the mother, which is why Jewishness follows the mother while shevet follows the father.

title.en: Emunah from 'em'; denial as rationalization

summary.en: From the rule that a noun drops the final nun of its verb (shen, gan), the Mashgiach shows that emunah is tied to 'em', mother. He concludes that every Jew believes, and that denial is rationalization, like Eisav blaming his wife for losing the brachos.

catalogTitle: מבשרי אחזה אלוקי

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem cannot be grasped by philosophy, since human intellect is not a sense made for G-dliness, yet a person can recognize that there is a Creator by looking at the wonders of his own body, as in 'from my flesh I see G-d'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach distinguishes two paths to emunah: the inherited, instinctive faith of Jews as believers descended from believers, and chakirah, philosophical inquiry, the path of the Rambam in his Moreh Nevuchim. He describes the dispute over philosophy, with the sages of Ashkenaz, especially the Rosh, forbidding it, and notes that philosophy is a foreign import found nowhere in Chumash, Shas or Midrash; the Acharonim, the Vilna Gaon among them, distanced themselves from it entirely. Philosophy fails, he explains, because the intellect is no more made to perceive Hashem than the ear is made to see a picture. The faculty for G-dliness is ruach hakodesh, present in every Jew through his neshamah but insulated by aveiros. Still, from the creations one can recognize that there is a Creator: 'from my flesh I see G-d'. He describes the eye, heart, blood vessels, lungs and digestion, an anatomy book, and a watch that could never assemble itself.

en: There are two paths to emunah: the inherited, felt faith of Jews as believers descended from believers, and chakirah, philosophical inquiry, as the Rambam did in Moreh Nevuchim.

Philosophy is a foreign import: no argument proving Hashem's existence by logic is found in Chumash, Shas or Midrash, and the Rishonim of Ashkenaz and later the Acharonim distanced themselves from it.
The intellect cannot grasp Hashem, just as no amount of hearing can hear a picture; the faculty for G-dliness is ruach hakodesh.
Every Jew has ruach hakodesh because of his neshamah, but aveiros insulate the body from the neshamah like insulation on a live wire.
Through the creations, though not in His essence, one can understand that there is a Ribono shel Olam, and a person need only look at his own body: 'from my flesh I see G-d'.

The eye, heart, blood vessels, lungs and digestive system each adjust and repair themselves automatically, and one cannot say they made themselves, just as shaking watch parts will never produce a watch.

from my flesh I see G-d

title.en: Two paths to emunah: feeling and inquiry

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that Jews are believers descended from believers, holding emunah as an instinctive inheritance from the Avos. He then presents the second path, chakirah, logical inquiry, and describes the Rambam's Moreh Nevuchim as its chief example, approaching Hashem, Torah from Heaven and reward and punishment through reason.

title.en: The dispute over philosophy

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how Rishonim attacked the Rambam's approach, how the sages of Ashkenaz, especially the Rosh, forbade philosophy and even made a cherem, while the Sefardi sages valued it. He stresses that philosophy is found nowhere in Chumash, Shas or Midrash, that the Acharonim, including the Vilna Gaon, rejected it entirely, and that Hashem cannot be 'figured out' like a mathematical problem.

title.en: Five senses, intellect and ruach hakodesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that our five senses connect us to our surroundings but none is made for G-dliness, and the intellect is likewise the wrong faculty, like trying to hear a picture. The sense for G-dliness is ruach hakodesh, present in every Jew through his neshamah; aveiros insulate a person from it like insulation on a live wire.

title.en: From my flesh I see G-d: the eye

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Acharonim warned against philosophy today, yet through Hashem's creations, though not His essence, one can understand that there is a Creator. Citing Iyov's 'from my flesh I see G-d', he describes the eye in detail: the retina, lens and pupil that adjusts to light, the eyelashes and tears that protect and clean it, its self-healing, and two eyes working together for depth.

title.en: The heart, blood, lungs and digestion

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the heart, a plain piece of muscle that beats for a lifetime and speeds up and slows down by itself, the fifty thousand miles of blood vessels that carry food and oxygen and remove waste, the lungs that adjust automatically, and the digestive system beginning with the teeth, asking whether all this came about by itself.

title.en: The anatomy book and the watch

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds the sense of taste and saliva, then tells of an anatomy book he found in an apartment in Eretz Yisrael, with wonders on every page such as why the spine is curved. He closes with the parable of a watch whose parts could never assemble themselves in a shaking machine, concluding that even a non-Jew should recognize the Creator simply by looking at his own body.

catalogTitle: הכרה של אמונה ע"י נפלאות הבריאה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows from the wonders and the precise balance of nature, the human body and history that the world cannot have come about by itself, and that people who claim it did are rationalizing so as not to see the Ribono shel Olam.

abstract.en: Continuing from his earlier talk on the wonders of the human body, the Mashgiach widens the view to all of nature: plants and animals depend on each other for oxygen and carbon dioxide, and the planets are held in a balance that a small shift would destroy. He brings the parable of the Chovos HaLevavos about a magnificent picture that someone claimed came from spilled ink, and calls the belief that the world made itself an even greater madness, a rationalization. He illustrates this with a story from Telz: a member of a club of maskilim stopped coming after a halacha about burying a dead man's blood revealed the Ribono shel Olam, because it took away his peace of mind. The Mashgiach then brings more wonders: the fixed 21 percent of oxygen in the air, cells that renew themselves except those of the brain, blood clotting, and water that expands as it freezes so that ice floats. He closes with Hashem's guidance seen in history and in the protection of every small child.

en: All parts of nature depend on each other, like the systems of the body: plants give off oxygen for animals and live from what animals give off, and the planets are held in a delicate balance.
Saying the world came about by itself is a greater madness than saying a masterpiece came from spilled ink; it is a rationalization.
People avoid seeing the Ribono shel Olam because recognizing Him would take away their freedom to do as they please.
The exact makeup of the air, the renewal of cells, blood clotting and the unusual behavior of water as it freezes are all wonders of the Ribono shel Olam that keep life possible.
Just as Hashem is seen in physics, He is seen in history, especially Jewish history, in current events and in the protection of every child.

candidateTopics: Chovos HaLevavos parable of the ink

title.en: The interdependence of all of nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that he spoke about the wonders of the body, and widens it to nature: animals and plants cannot exist without each other, exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide, and the planets are held in a balance that would collapse if one left its orbit.

title.en: The Chovos HaLevavos's parable of the ink

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chovos HaLevavos's parable of a magnificent picture that someone claimed was made by ink bottles spilled by the wind, and says that believing the world made itself is a greater madness. He calls it a rationalization and begins to recount how, during a war in Eretz Yisroel, even secular newspapers reported the miracles.

title.en: The club house in Telz

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story from a sefer about Telz: after a member of a club of maskilim took his own life, plaster kept falling from the ceiling until the Rosh Yeshiva's halacha about burying a dead man's blood was followed. One member then stopped coming, because seeing the Ribono shel Olam took away his peace of mind; the Mashgiach says one need not go to such a club house to see Him.

title.en: Oxygen, cells and blood clotting

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the air holds exactly 21 percent oxygen, enough to breathe and not so much that one match would set the world on fire. He then describes how the body's cells die and are replaced within seven years, except the brain cells that hold memory, and how a substance in the blood makes it clot so that a cut does not bleed a person to death.

title.en: Why ice floats

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every substance expands with heat and contracts with cold, as in a thermometer, but water near freezing reverses and expands, which is why a frozen bottle bursts. Because of this, ice stays on top of a river as a blanket and the fish below survive; were it otherwise the river would fill with ice from the bottom and all life in it would die.

title.en: Hashem in history and in raising children

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks whether, with millions of such wonders, one can say the world made itself, mentions sleep as another wonder, and says that just as Hashem is seen in physics He is seen in history, especially Jewish history, and in daily events. He ends with the protection Hashem gives every small child through countless dangers, so that the boys before him grew up healthy.

catalogTitle: רשב”י - The נשמה of משיח

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is the aspect of Moshiach and of Yovel, the great return, who abolishes mourning, heals the jealousy that destroyed the Beis HaMikdash, unites all Jews, and on Lag Ba'omer gives a real tikkun beyond Pesach Sheni.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the concept of Yovel, introduced in this week's sedra: Yovel means return, and its shofar, like the shofar of Ne'ilah and of Moshiach, brings every Jew back to his root. Even the eved nirtza, whom Shemitah cannot free, goes out at Yovel. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's mitzvah is Yovel; he is the aspect of Moshiach. Through the Rambam's signs of Moshiach and the end of mourning, the Mashgiach explains why Lag Ba'omer is pure joy, with stories from Meron. Rabbi Akiva's students died for lack of mutual respect, the jealousy rooted in the moon's complaint; Moshiach will repair it, and Rashbi, who can redeem even the lowest, unites all Jews as the Beis HaMikdash did. A mashal of the last tug teaches that each small mitzvah may complete the building. This year is special for geulah. Finally, Pesach Sheni gives a partial tikkun, while Lag Ba'omer, like Purim, looks forward to the Pesach of Moshiach.

en: Yovel means return: its shofar, like the shofar of Ne'ilah and the shofar of Moshiach, brings every Jew back to his root.
Every Jew has a mitzvah that is his root, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's mitzvah is Yovel; he is the aspect of Moshiach.
Moshiach abolishes mourning, and so the day of Rashbi's passing is a day of joy rather than mourning.
Rabbi Akiva's students died because they did not show each other respect, a jealousy rooted in the flaw of the moon, which Moshiach will repair.
The Beis HaMikdash was the place of unity and was destroyed by baseless hatred; Rashbi, who unites all Jews, is like the Beis HaMikdash.
Pesach Sheni, chesed shebehod, is only a substitute tikkun, while Lag Ba'omer, hod shebehod, gives a real tikkun, a Pesach of the future.

candidateTopics: jealousy and the flaw of the moon

title.en: Yovel, the great return

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces Yovel from this week's sedra: it means return, its shofar is like the shofar of Ne'ilah and of Moshiach, and it frees even the eved nirtza whom Shemitah cannot free. He concludes that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's mitzvah is Yovel and that he is the aspect of Moshiach.

title.en: Moshiach returns Jews and ends mourning

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam's sign of one who is presumed to be Moshiach, explaining it as bringing Jews back to their roots. He then explains that Moshiach abolishes mourning, and that on the day of Rashbi's passing one does not fast but rejoices.

title.en: No mourning in Meron; Rabbi Akiva's students

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a great Rebbe who had people dance in Meron on the fifth of Av, and Rabbi Chaim Vital's account of a man punished for saying Nachem at Rashbi's celebration. He then explains that Rashbi annulled the mourning for Rabbi Akiva's students, who died for not showing each other respect.

title.en: Jealousy, the flaw of the moon

summary.en: The Mashgiach traces jealousy to the moon's complaint against the sun and follows it through the snake, Kayin, Yosef's brothers and the kings of Israel. He notes there is no English word for being happy at another's success, and says Moshiach will repair the flaw of the moon.

title.en: Rashbi strengthens even the lowest

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a well-known saying that Rashbi gives strength even to the lowest, and the Gemara that Rashbi can exempt the whole world from judgment. He connects the end of jealousy between Ephraim and Yehudah with the baseless hatred that destroyed the Beis HaMikdash, which the Maharal calls the place of unity.

title.en: Coming to Rashbi is like coming to Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that Rashbi is the 'face of the Master, Hashem', so coming to him is like coming to the Beis HaMikdash, and in Meron every kind of Jew gathers. Yovel applies only when all Jews are together in the land, and Rashbi, who unites all Jews, is in the aspect of Yovel, which appears now in Behar and Bechukosai.

title.en: Kamtza and Bar Kamtza: the last tug

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Gemara tells the story of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza and brings a great tzaddik's mashal of strong men who loosened a tree that a child then pulled down. Kamtza and Bar Kamtza were the last tug after generations of hatred, and in the same way the last generation will give the last small tug to build the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: A year auspicious for geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a year in which Shabbos falls within Pesach is auspicious for geulah, and that this year Lag Ba'omer falls on Friday and carries into Shabbos, making it a stronger Lag Ba'omer. He warns against meddling in speculation about Moshiach: the task is to learn, daven, do chesed and do mitzvos.

title.en: Pesach Sheni and the tumah of tzaddikim

summary.en: After a Zohar on the whispered command in Emor, the Mashgiach brings the Zohar that Pesach Sheni is only a substitute for those who missed the first Pesach. He asks how that fits the Gemara that they were tzaddikim, and brings the Yismach Moshe: the graves of tzaddikim do not defile, but the Torah could not write so since no one knows who is a tzaddik; only Moshe Rabbeinu, who could ask Hashem, could decide.

title.en: From Pesach Sheni to Lag Ba'omer, and Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the Bnos Tzelofchad and explains that those who asked were really permitted, while Pesach Sheni was given for later generations. Pesach Sheni, chesed shebehod, is a partial tikkun, but Lag Ba'omer, hod shebehod, gives a real Pesach. Through the At-Bash calendar rule he shows that Purim looks forward to the Pesach of Moshiach, and Lag Ba'omer falls on Purim's weekday.

title.en: Nefesh, ruach, neshamah: two promises of Yovel

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that a flaw in deed, speech or thought shows in one's property, wife or children. Yovel promises two returns, to one's property and to one's family; Pesach Sheni brings only the lower return of property, while Lag Ba'omer brings the higher one.

catalogTitle: התבוננות בנפלאות הבריאה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that in our time, when open miracles are not seen, the mitzvah is to believe, yet one who contemplates his surroundings can still see wonders, such as the striking number of Kohanim and Levi'im among the great teachers of halachah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that today we see no great revelations or miracles, while our grandparents told reliable stories of tzaddikim. He tells one such story, recorded by the Maharsham's son: the Maharsham, a great masmid as a young man, fell gravely ill; a messenger was sent to Reb Ayzikl of Zidichov, and at that very hour the Maharsham saw his heavenly judgment, where a dark angel blew his Torah off the scale until a young black-bearded dayan defended Torah learned even not purely for Heaven's sake. Later he recognized that dayan as Reb Ayzikl, who told him to always be lenient for Jews. The Mashgiach then explains that today the mitzvah is to believe, and believing is greater than seeing, as the Kotzker Rebbe answered. Still, contemplating our surroundings shows wonders: Moshe Rabbeinu's blessing that Levi would teach Torah to Israel is visible in how many Kohanim and Levi'im are among the commentators on Shulchan Aruch, the later poskim, the Brisk line and even the roshei yeshiva in the beis medrash.

en: Today there are no open miracles because the mitzvah of our time is emunah, and believing is greater than seeing.
Not every story of tzaddikim is reliable, since many were embellished or invented, but some were recorded by trustworthy people and can be relied on.
In the Maharsham's story, the Torah he had learned saved him in the heavenly judgment, because even Torah not learned purely for Heaven's sake is precious above in a time of deep exile.
One who contemplates his surroundings can see wonders today as well, which show that there is a Ribono shel Olam.

Moshe Rabbeinu's blessing that the tribe of Levi will teach Torah to Israel is fulfilled to this day in the disproportionate number of Kohanim and Levi'im among the great poskim and teachers of Torah.

the tribe of Levi as teachers of Torah
the Kotzker Rebbe and the ushpizin

title.en: Stories of tzaddikim and the Maharsham's diligence

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that today no great miracles are seen, while our grandparents told reliable stories of tzaddikim. He introduces the Maharsham, a great posek known for leniency, asks where this came from, and describes how the Minchas Chinuch told him at his semichah to learn constantly, even in spare minutes on Shabbos.

title.en: The Maharsham's illness and heavenly judgment

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the young Maharsham fell gravely ill, a messenger was sent to Reb Ayzikl of Zidichov, and at the crisis he saw his judgment in Heaven: a dark angel blew his Torah off the scale until a black-bearded young dayan defended Torah learned even not for its own sake. Later he recognized Reb Ayzikl as that dayan and was told to always be lenient for Jews, which the Mashgiach says explains the Maharsham's leniency.

title.en: Believing is greater than seeing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that today the mitzvah is to believe, and tells how the Kotzker Rebbe answered a tzaddik who claimed to see the ushpizin with his eyes: he believes they come, and believing is greater than seeing. Yet contemplating our surroundings reveals wonders, and he begins his example: Moshe Rabbeinu's blessing that Levi will teach Torah, and the Chemdas Shlomo's observation that almost all the commentators on Shulchan Aruch are from Levi.

title.en: Kohanim and Levi'im as Israel's teachers

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the Shulchan Aruch and its commentators, the later poskim and the Brisk line of roshei yeshiva, showing how many are Kohanim or Levi'im, far beyond their share of the people, and notes that Chassidic Rebbes come from the house of David. He counts the roshei yeshiva sitting at the mizrach wall, finds seven Kohanim and Levi'im against four Yisraelim, and concludes that one sees here the truth of the Torah, three and a half thousand years after Moshe Rabbeinu's blessing.

catalogTitle: התבוננות בנפלאות התורה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that even in a generation without open miracles, the endless depth of the Torah, which a child and the greatest gadol learn from the same Chumash and Gemara, is itself a wonder that proves it comes from Heaven, and that Hashem reveals Himself to whoever opens his eyes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that in the generation before Moshiach one no longer sees the open wonders earlier generations saw, and the test is to believe without seeing. Yet whoever reflects can see wonders even now, above all in the Torah, which Dovid HaMelech asked to see and called sweeter than honey; one who does not taste it is like a sick patient who blames the food. He then contrasts a schoolchild's textbooks, replaced every year as he outgrows them, with the Chumash and Gemara that a child, a rosh yeshiva and the great Acharonim all learn, each seeing new things. The answer is that Torah comes from the Infinite and is itself endless, with four layers of PaRDeS, while a secular book ends at the page. Seeing this requires that Hashem open one's eyes, as with Hagar and the Chashmona'im's jar of oil. Finally, like Avraham Avinu who recognized the Owner of the lit palace, whoever strengthens his emunah will see Hashem's wonders in his daily life, for which Jews thank Him in Modim.

en: In this generation there are no open revelations, and the test is to believe without seeing; yet one who reflects can still see wonders that cry out that there is a Creator and that the Torah is true.
The Torah is sweet, and one who does not taste its sweetness has lost his sense of taste, like a sick patient who blames the hospital food.
Secular textbooks are outgrown and replaced every year, while the same Chumash and Gemara serve a child, a rosh yeshiva and the greatest Torah giants, each seeing new things in them.
Because the Torah comes from the Infinite, it is itself endless, with four layers of depth (pshat, remez, drush, sod), while a secular book ends at the page.
One can look at a thing and not see it until Hashem opens one's eyes, as with Hagar and the well and the Greeks who did not see the sealed jar of oil.
Everything that happens to a Jew, down to a single day, is full of wonders, and whoever strengthens his emunah will see Hashem revealing Himself through them.

title.en: Wonders hidden in our generation; the sweetness of Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that today one no longer sees open wonders and the test is to believe without seeing, but one who reflects can still see wonders, above all in the Torah. He brings Dovid HaMelech's request to see the wonders of the Torah and his praise of its sweetness, compares one who does not taste it to a sick patient who blames the food, and explains that both the Written and the Oral Torah are from Heaven.

title.en: Schoolbooks are outgrown; the Chumash and Gemara are not

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how an American child gets new, thicker textbooks every grade through college because the old ones become too elementary. A Jewish child, by contrast, keeps the same Chumash all his life, and the Bava Metzia he learned at nine he learns again at thirteen and eighteen as an entirely different study; it is the same Gemara learned by the great Acharonim and Rishonim, sealed by Ravina and Rav Ashi and given to Moshe Rabbeinu at Sinai.

title.en: Why the Torah never runs out: from the Infinite

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a secular book must be replaced while a Chumash or Gemara can be learned again and again with new discoveries, and answers that the Torah comes from the Infinite and is therefore endless. No human could create a wisdom that is simple for a child and deep for a genius; this itself is a wonder. He explains the four layers of PaRDeS, noting that even later Amoraim lost the power of drush, and contrasts this with secular wisdom that is only surface.

title.en: Looking without seeing: Hagar and the jar of oil

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Hagar, who did not see the well beside her dying son until Hashem opened her eyes, and the Greeks who defiled all the oil in the Heichal but did not see the jar sealed by the Kohen Gadol. He says one who learns Torah honestly, davens well and guards himself from sin will have his eyes opened, and that not only the Torah but everything that happens to a Jew each day is full of wonders.

title.en: Avraham and the lit palace; daily miracles in Modim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash of a man who saw a lit palace in the wilderness until its owner revealed himself, applied to Avraham Avinu who saw the order of the world and history until Hashem revealed Himself to him. So too whoever strengthens his emunah and fear of Heaven will see Hashem in the wonders of his Torah and his day, and the Mashgiach points to Modim, said three times daily, where Jews thank Hashem for His daily miracles.

catalogTitle: חנוכה - שורש החקירה מהיונים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach traces philosophy back to the Greeks, who denied the natural instinct of emunah and replaced it with the worship of physical strength and beauty, and presents Chanukah as the fight against that substitute.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the great Torah thinkers wrote works of chakirah (philosophical inquiry) only because Jewish intellectuals in Arab lands were drawn after gentile philosophy, whose root is Greek wisdom; the Torah itself never sets out to prove that there is a Creator. Citing the Bnei Yissaschar, he explains that one who 'tests' both sides is, for that moment, a kofer, and that the siddur puts Ein k'Elokeinu before Mi k'Elokeinu for this reason. Philosophy, he says, is mental acrobatics: like a chess champion, any philosopher can be refuted by a bigger mind. The Greeks set up reason as the only thing to believe, to throw off the yoke. But Hashem created an instinct of emunah in every person, just as He created appetite, and an instinct must be satisfied. So the Greeks made idols of physical strength and beauty, the root of sport and fashion. Chanukah, whose gematria equals guf, fought this. He closes by urging bochurim to make a cheshbon hanefesh.

en: The Torah never sets out to prove that there is a Creator; the Jewish works of chakirah were written only to counter gentile philosophy that attracted Jewish intellectuals.
Philosophy cannot reach absolute truth: whatever proofs one thinker brings, a greater mind can come and refute them.
Hashem created in every person an instinct of emunah, just as He created the appetite for food, because without trust neither personal nor social life could exist.
Having rejected emunah in G-d, the Greeks still had to satisfy that instinct, so they deified physical strength and beauty.
The Chashmona'im fought against these two substitutes for emunah, and the message of Chanukah is that victory comes not through might but through the spirit of Hashem.

title.en: Why Torah giants wrote works of chakirah

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the earlier discussion of the Jewish philosophers led by the Rambam and the controversy over his books, notes that the Torah never tries to prove the Creator's existence, and explains that these works were needed because Jewish intellectuals in Arab lands were drawn after gentile philosophy rooted in Greek wisdom.

title.en: Testing both sides, and philosophy as mental acrobatics

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that one who weighs, in the philosophical way, whether there is a Ribono shel Olam is a kofer at that moment, and explains why the siddur says Ein k'Elokeinu before Mi k'Elokeinu. He then calls philosophy mental acrobatics and compares it to chess champions: any proof can be overturned by a greater mind.

title.en: Greek philosophy and the instinct of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach traces philosophy to Greece and explains that its axiom, to believe only what reason proves, was a way to throw off the yoke. Against this he shows that Hashem created an instinct of emunah in every person, just like appetite, without which buying milk or asking a stranger the time would be impossible; the Greeks, whom the Chashmona'im fought, tried to nullify it.

title.en: Idols of strength and beauty

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every instinct must be gratified, illustrating with what a psychologist told him about feeding through a zipper in the stomach. Since the Greeks would not believe in G-d, who would bind them, they made idols of physical strength and beauty; from this came the Olympics and athletics, and the hero-worship of athletes today.

title.en: Chanukah against the worship of the body

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Chashmona'im fought with mesirus nefesh against the two substitutes for emunah, beauty and strength of the body, the worship of beauty showing also in designer clothing. Just as Moshiach equals nachash in gematria, Chanukah equals guf; the haftarah's 'not by might nor by strength but by My spirit' is its message, and the Greeks' idols in the Beis HaMikdash were what the victory removed.

title.en: Kelipas Yavan today and a Chanukah cheshbon hanefesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach laments that the Greek kelipah of sports heroes and designer fashion has entered the batei medrash, explains with the Gemara's 'today he says do this' how it leads step by step toward avodah zarah, contrasts an elder who kept his wedding Shabbos garment all his life, and calls on bochurim to make a cheshbon hanefesh on Chanukah.

catalogTitle: The Light of יובל Begins to be Revealed

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yovel, the power of return, reaches even the lowest Jewish souls that Shabbos cannot help, and that its light begins to shine in the week of Hod and on Lag Ba'omer.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews how the soul, a part of G-d above, descends through many contractions, and how holy sparks fell into the klipos through the breaking of the vessels. Following the Tanya's parable of the body, he describes the souls of each generation from head to toenails: the attached part of the nail is the sinner still bound to Yiddishkeit, the protruding part is the heretic cut off before Shabbos. Shabbos and Shemitah free the Eved Ivri, who sold himself to the Sitra Achra, the 'maidservant that inherits her mistress'; but one who refuses Shabbos is released only by Yovel, the law of return. Shavuos, the fiftieth day, is a small Yovel, as shown by Rus who 'returned'. Pesach Sheni opens the week of Hod and Lag Ba'omer, Hod sheb'Hod, closes it: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, like the Beis HaMikdash, gathers all Jews, and this year Lag Ba'omer extends into Shabbos.

en: Every soul, even the lowest, remains bound to its source, as even the toenails draw from the brain in the Tanya's parable.
The attached part of the nail stands for sinners still bound to Yiddishkeit; the protruding part stands for heretics, cut off before Shabbos.
Shabbos and Shemitah free the Eved Ivri from the Sitra Achra, but one who clings to his servitude is freed only by Yovel.
Yovel is the law of return: every Jewish soul, even one discarded like a cut nail, will ultimately return with the shofar of Moshiach.
Pesach Sheni at the start of the week of Hod and Lag Ba'omer at its end are second chances, when the light of Yovel is already seen.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is like the Beis HaMikdash and the Kohen Gadol: a place of unity, where there is no mourning and all Jews come together.

title.en: Contractions, broken vessels and holy sparks

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews that the soul is a part of G-d above that comes down through contractions, using the parable of pouring wine from a barrel into a bottle. He explains the breaking of the vessels, the sparks that fell into the klipos, and how a Jew frees them by using his food, clothing and home for the service of Hashem.

title.en: From the head to the toenails

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the soul's coverings to insulation on a wire and brings the Tanya's parable of the body, where even the toenails remain bound to the brain. He applies it to the souls of each generation and distinguishes two levels of nail: the attached part, sinners still bound to Yiddishkeit, and the protruding part, heretics, which is cut off before Shabbos.

title.en: The Eved Ivri and the maidservant

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Eved Ivri, permitted to a maidservant, has fallen into the Sitra Achra and lost his Jewish lineage. He brings the passuk in Mishlei about the maidservant who inherits her mistress and explains it as the power of evil dominating in exile, when the nations take the bounty first.

title.en: Yaakov and Esav, Yerushalayim and Rome

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the constant war between Yaakov and Esav, from the birth when Yaakov held Esav's heel, to the rivalry of Yerushalayim and Rome. He brings the Tzvi LaTzaddik that Yerushalayim is spelled without a yud in exile, and that Moshiach will add it; Shabbos frees the Eved Ivri from the maidservant's grip.

title.en: Yovel, the law of return, and Rus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why nails are cut before Shabbos: they are the Jew so sunk in the Sitra Achra that he refuses Shabbos's rescue. Yet no Jew is lost forever; Yovel returns him to Klal Yisrael. Shavuos, the fiftieth day, is a small Yovel, which is why Rus, a Jewish soul born in Moav who 'returned', is read then; the shofar of Moshiach will bring back every soul.

title.en: The week of Hod and Pesach Sheni

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the days of Sefirah prepare for the fiftieth day: five weeks refine the middos and the last two polish them, so the work is essentially done with Hod. The week of Hod opens with Pesach Sheni, a second chance for those who were impure, with the light of Yovel already visible; he brings the teaching about a convert and the Korban Pesach.

title.en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pesach and milah, the only positive mitzvos carrying kareis, bind a Jew to Hashem. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is the aspect of building the Beis HaMikdash, which stands for unity and was destroyed through baseless hatred; Yovel too requires all Jews together. Like the Kohen Gadol, who does not mourn, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai has no mourning.

title.en: No mourning in Meron; Hod sheb'Hod

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rav Chaim Vital's account of a disciple of the Arizal who said Nachem on Lag Ba'omer and was punished. He compares Meron to the Kosel, the two places that draw the whole spectrum of Jews, and explains Hod sheb'Hod as the lowest level, where holiness is strong enough to reach the very bottom.

title.en: The gates are open

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that a heavenly crier announces the gates are open, and the Ba'al HaTanya that the Yom Kippur tekiah is the shofar of Yovel. He explains that a taste of Yovel reaches even the lowest Jews on Lag Ba'omer, who feel it tugging at their hearts, and says Hashem is now beckoning everyone to come in and take Torah, tefillah and closeness.

title.en: Lag Ba'omer on Friday stays for Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls this a special year, citing the Chasam Sofer, and notes that Lag Ba'omer falls on Friday. A Yom Tov on Friday stays into Shabbos, as Shabbos kept Adam HaRishon in Gan Eden according to Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer, so there are two days of Lag Ba'omer, two days of the great shofar of Yovel.

catalogTitle: אמונה של כלל ישראל תלוי במעמד הר סיני

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mitzvah of emunah rests on the mesorah of Maamad Har Sinai, where Hashem spoke to an entire nation, unlike every other faith that rests on one individual.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks what the halachos of the mitzvah of emunah are: just as a sukkah must be built according to its halachos, emunah, which the Rambam counts among the 613 mitzvos, has its own laws. The instinct of faith, contemplating nature and philosophical inquiry were discussed earlier; now he turns to the Rambam in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah. First he gives the gist: something one individual reports can be doubted, but an event witnessed by multitudes cannot be denied, as with George Washington or Julius Caesar. Other religions rest on one man and his charisma or wonders, while the Torah was given before millions at Sinai and handed down by the whole people. He then learns the Rambam: Moshe was not believed because of his signs, which he performed for practical needs, but because of Sinai, where Hashem spoke face to face with the nation. A later navi is believed only because Moshe commanded it, as witnesses are believed by Hashem's command.

en: Emunah is one of the 613 mitzvos, so like every mitzvah it has halachos, and the Rambam sets them out in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah.
What one individual claims can be believed or doubted, but an event that happened before multitudes cannot be denied by any reasonable person.
Other religions rest on a single founder who swayed people with his character or wonders, while the Jewish people believe in no individual.
At Sinai Hashem revealed Himself to millions, who all heard Him directly and passed it down to their children; this mesorah of a whole people is unique.
According to the Rambam, Moshe Rabbeinu was not believed because of his signs, which he performed out of need, but because of Maamad Har Sinai.
A later navi, like witnesses in beis din, is believed not because of his wonders but because the Torah commands it; the mitzvah of emunah itself is the mesorah.

title.en: The halachos of the mitzvah of emunah

summary.en: After a question on Rashi about the first mitzvah, the Mashgiach asks what the halachos of emunah are, comparing it to a sukkah that must follow its halachos. He reviews the ways to emunah discussed earlier and turns to the Rambam, noting that in the Yad the Rambam speaks as halacha, unlike the Moreh Nevuchim.

title.en: A public event cannot be denied

summary.en: The Mashgiach states that the Jewish emunah comes from Sinai and cannot be questioned, and sets out the rule: an individual's report may be doubted, but a public event may not. He illustrates with George Washington and Julius Caesar, whose existence and deeds no sane person denies even if many stories about them are false.

title.en: Other faiths rest on one man; Sinai on a nation

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Christianity and Islam, each founded on one individual who swayed people with charisma or wonders, with the Torah, given before millions at Har Sinai who all heard Hashem and passed it down. Even other religions accept the Torah because they cannot deny it, claiming only that it was later replaced.

title.en: The Rambam: not signs but Sinai

summary.en: The Mashgiach learns the Rambam in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah chapter 8: belief based on signs leaves a doubt, and Moshe's wonders were done for practical needs. Belief in Moshe comes from Sinai, where the people saw with their own eyes and Hashem spoke 'face to face' with all of them, and no lie can be handed to later generations without protest.

title.en: Believing a navi, like believing witnesses

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a later navi is believed not for his wonders but because Moshe commanded it, just as beis din believes two witnesses although they might lie, as in the case of Navos. He concludes that the other ways to emunah only support it, while the mitzvah itself is the mesorah, and says the Rambam will be continued next week.

catalogTitle: האומות מכירים וכופרים מטעם של rationalization

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains from the Rambam that our belief in the Torah rests on the mesorah of Har Sinai, so no later prophet can change it, and that the nations, who know this, deny it through rationalization born of jealousy.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the mesorah of Klal Yisroel is true because a whole nation heard Hashem at Har Sinai, and that a prophet is believed only because the Torah commands it, like two witnesses. With the Rambam in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah he shows that a prophet with signs who contradicts Moshe is not heeded, as witnesses who say it is night are not believed by one who sees daylight. The Torah cannot be added to or changed, so the claims of the nations about a new law collapse; Bilaam himself said Hashem does not change His mind. Why do they hold on? Rationalization and jealousy of the chosen people. The Mashgiach applies this to Rashi's question about the first mitzvah, to Moshe as father of all prophets, and to the world's preoccupation with Jews and Yerushalayim. A story of a dying heretic who recanted shows that rationalization falls away at the end. He closes that mesorah is the halachic basis of emunah.

en: Belief in a prophet after Moshe is only a decree of the Torah, like believing two witnesses, while belief in Moshe rests on what the whole nation saw at Har Sinai.
A prophet who comes with wonders to contradict Moshe is not heeded, just as a court that sees daylight does not believe witnesses who say it is night.
The Torah cannot be added to, reduced or exchanged, so any claim that Hashem gave a new Torah is false by the very Torah its claimants accept.
The nations hold on to their claims through rationalization, driven above all by jealousy of the Jewish people as the chosen nation.
Even mitzvos given to Avraham and the Avos are kept only because Moshe wrote them in the Torah; Moshe is the father of the prophets before him and after him.
Mesorah, not philosophy, is the halachic basis of emunah, and it is the strongest of the ways to faith.
